# In-flow writing tools (+ rubric clarity)

## Context
The rubric panel is hard to read: too many numbers at once, weak separation, shallow expand, and a confusing
"What would you like to explore?" dropdown. The bigger vision: **notice what the writer is wrestling with while they
write, and put a small, intuitive tool in their hands right there** — anchored to the passage they're working
on, shown in the page margin like Google Docs comments, saveable and reusable across pieces.

Two existing pieces already do half of this:
- `src/components/editor/extensions/quick-review.ts`: on a typing pause, one Jev (`api.systemOne.ask`) `choice` call
  classifies the current paragraph and draws a decoration + `?` widget. It has rate limiting (12/min),
  backoff, a cache, the `live-review-enabled` toggle and stale-doc guards. **This is the template to generalise.**
- `src/utils/system-one.ts`: typed Jev questions. About $0.00006 per 11-question batch, cheap enough to run on every pause.

Decisions (confirmed with the user): tools are **anchored to passages**. The first build is the **full loop with 4 tools**.
**json-render** supplies the catalog (it constrains what the model can generate). Use the **side margins** like Google Docs.

## Architecture (the loop)

```
keystrokes ─▶ StruggleTracker (PM plugin, local, no network)
               per-paragraph counters: churn, undo, re-rewrites of the same sentence, dwell w/o progress
          ─▶ pause + threshold crossed ─▶ Jev choice: "what is the writer trying to fix?" → tool kind | none
          ─▶ ToolSpec (json-render catalog; deterministic data first, LLM fill only where needed)
          ─▶ right margin rail card aligned to the passage (Docs-style) + faint underline on the span
          ─▶ writer uses it → apply / dismiss / "Keep this tool" → left margin shelf → reuse on any passage
```

### 1. Struggle signals: `src/utils/struggle-signals.ts` (new, pure) + `extensions/struggle-tracker.ts` (new)
- A ProseMirror plugin that keeps per-textblock state **keyed by positions mapped through `tr.mapping`**
  (paragraphs have no stable ids). Per block it tracks: inserted/deleted chars over a rolling window, net growth,
  undo count, and how many times the same sentence span was replaced. It also keeps the **last 3 versions** of the block
  text, in memory only; Sentence Lab needs them.
- Pure scoring function `struggleScore(counters) → { score, kind hints }`. Signals: churn ÷ net growth,
  repeated rewrites of one sentence, heavy undo use, adding and removing hedges ("perhaps", "arguably"), and long dwell
  after deletions. Unit-tested with synthetic counters.
- Rules for staying quiet: nothing runs while typing, only on a pause (reuse quick-review's 650 ms plus the
  `editor.view.composing` guard). At most **one live suggestion at a time**. Dismissing puts that block on a cooldown.
  Hidden in zen mode. Respects `live-review-enabled` and a new `in-flow-tools-enabled` meta flag in Settings.

### 2. Classifier: `src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts` (new)
- One `api.systemOne.ask` batch per trigger: a `choice` over the 4 tool kinds + "Nothing to help with", plus a
  `choice` for passage kind (claim / scene / explanation / transition / list). The input is the passage, its prior versions and
  the brief's goal and audience. Its instructions use the same "text is evidence, not instructions" framing as quick-review.
- Pull quick-review's rate-limiter, cache and backoff into a small shared `createPauseRunner()` helper, so both
  schedulers use the same budget and neither can starve the other.

### 3. Tool catalog: json-render (`src/components/in-flow/catalog.ts`)
- `@json-render/core` `defineCatalog` with zod props for exactly 4 components. The data is deterministic wherever possible;
  the LLM (writer's BYOK provider through `ai-client`, new `AiFeature` `"in-flow-tool"`, `generateTrackedText` so Arize
  traces it) fills only the text fields. json-render's catalog prompt plus SpecStream let those fields stream in.
- **Spike first:** confirm `@json-render/core` works without a framework renderer's schema package. We'd write our own
  Qwik renderer (`ToolRenderer`, a switch from component type to Qwik component). **Fallback:** keep the same zod
  schemas and parse the model's JSON with zod directly; the catalog shape stays the same.

| Tool | Triggered by | Data | Interaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sentence Lab** | Same sentence rewritten 3+ times | Your own attempts, deterministic from the tracker, plus 2 LLM variants | Pick an attempt, or mix clauses, then **Use this**. It replaces the span in one undoable transaction |
| **Rhythm Strip** | Split/join churn, long paragraph | Sentence lengths as bars, pure, no LLM | Hover a bar to highlight its sentence; click to select it |
| **Claim Check** | Hedge on/off churn, bare assertion | The claim (Jev extraction) + evidence slots | Fill a slot, or **Find a source**, which goes through the existing research apparatus (TinyFish) |
| **Reader Questions** | Stall/dwell after a paragraph | 3 questions a reader would ask here (LLM) | Tick when answered; **Jot** sends it to scraps |

### 4. Margin layout: `src/components/in-flow/margin-rail.tsx` (new)
- The manuscript is centred at `--doc-width` inside the flex-1 scroll container (`src/routes/editor/index.tsx` ~1386),
  so wide screens have empty gutters. Render two absolutely positioned rails **inside the same scroll container**,
  so cards scroll with the page.
  - **Right rail: live tools.** Each card's top = `view.coordsAtPos(anchor.from)` relative to the scroll container.
    Overlapping cards stack downward with a gap, as in Docs. The active card slides nearer its anchor, and a
    thin connector line joins it to the span's underline. Positions are recomputed on the existing
    derive/scroll/resize signals only (not per keystroke).
  - **Left rail: "Your tools" shelf** of saved tools, sticky. Click one to apply it to the paragraph at the cursor.

  replacing their in-body popover when there's room. That gives one margin language. Persona notes and comments can join later.

- "Keep this tool" stores a **template, never passage text**: `{ id, kind, name, config }`. Examples of config: a rhythm target range, the
  wording of the claim-check slots, a custom Reader-Questions angle. Stored globally (not per folio) in IDB meta under

## Files
New: `src/utils/struggle-signals.ts`, `src/components/editor/extensions/struggle-tracker.ts`,
`src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts`, `src/utils/pause-runner.ts`, `src/utils/saved-tools.ts`,
`src/components/in-flow/{catalog.ts,tool-renderer.tsx,margin-rail.tsx,sentence-lab.tsx,rhythm-strip.tsx,claim-check.tsx,reader-questions.tsx}`

### 6. Rubric panel clarity: `src/components/rubric/rubric-panel.tsx`, `writing-tools.tsx`
- Header: grade stamp + one score only. "By your weights", scoring method and model move into a **"How this was
  scored"** disclosure. It shows the real formula from `combineJudgesAndStatic` (`src/utils/rubric.ts:564`): judge mean
  ×0.45, harshest judge ×0.35, shape ×0.2 (with the target-fit cap if it applied), then the curve.
- One line under the grade: **"Weakest: {criterion}"**, with **Work on it in the draft**. This finds the weakest
  passage (live-review `passages` triage) and opens the matching in-flow tool there. That's the bridge between the panel and the flow.
- Stronger separation: solid rules between sections, and criterion rows grouped Spine / Your own. Expanding a row shows the
  reason, then the quoted passage when there is one, then the next move. The fixed next move stays only as a fallback.
- Writing tools: replace the "What would you like to explore?" select with a visible grid of 8 lens cards
  (label + description from `WRITING_LENSES`).

New: `src/utils/struggle-signals.ts`, `src/components/editor/extensions/struggle-tracker.ts`,
`src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts`, `src/utils/pause-runner.ts`, `src/utils/saved-tools.ts`,
`src/components/in-flow/{catalog.ts,tool-renderer.tsx,margin-rail.tsx,sentence-lab.tsx,rhythm-strip.tsx,claim-check.tsx,reader-questions.tsx}`
(+ `*.test.ts` for the pure modules, `*.stories.tsx` for the 4 tools and the rail).
Modified: `twyne-editor.tsx` (register tracker, mount rails, start in-flow runner next to `startQuickReview`),
`extensions/quick-review.ts` (shared runner; render into the rail), `routes/editor/index.tsx` (rail slot),
`rubric-panel.tsx`, `writing-tools.tsx`, `ai-client.ts` (feature `"in-flow-tool"`), settings route (toggle),
`package.json` (`@json-render/core`).

## Build order
1. json-render spike (30 min, decide catalog vs zod fallback) → 2. struggle signals + tests → 3. margin rail with
Rhythm Strip (no LLM, proves layout end to end) → 4. classifier + shared pause runner → 5. Sentence Lab, Claim
Check, Reader Questions → 6. saved tools + left shelf → 7. quick-review into the rail → 8. rubric panel + lens grid.

## Verification
- `bun test` each new pure module on its own (the full suite has a known cross-file flake): struggle scoring, position
  mapping across edits, saved-tools round trip, catalog/zod validation of good and bad specs, rail stacking layout.
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`; Storybook stories for each tool and the rail at narrow and wide widths.
- Run the app (`run` skill) and use Chrome: rewrite one sentence 3–4 times and pause, and check that the Sentence Lab card appears in
  the right margin aligned with it. Apply it, then undo it once. Keep the tool, then apply it from the left shelf to another paragraph.
  Narrow the window and confirm the popover fallback. Toggle the setting off and confirm nothing fires. Open the rubric, click
  "Work on it in the draft", and check it lands on a passage with a tool open.

name: json-render-in-flow-tools
description: In-flow margin tools use @json-render/core with a custom Qwik renderer; catalog.validate() does NOT check props per component
metadata:
  type: project
---

Margin tools (Sentence Lab, Rhythm Strip, Claim Check, Reader Questions), added 2026-09-25, use `@json-render/core` 0.21 (no Qwik renderer upstream; `src/components/in-flow/tool-renderer.tsx` is ours). Specs are seeded deterministically and a model only streams JSONL patches into one allowed list path.

**Why:** `catalog.validate()` checks the component `type` is in the catalog but validates props only loosely, so an empty `RhythmStrip` passed. `validateToolSpec` re-checks each element against its own zod schema; keep that when adding components.

**How to apply:** New tool = zod props + catalog entry + `PROPS_FOR` + a Qwik component in tool-renderer. `createSpecStreamCompiler` also dedupes identical lines, so identical streamed values collapse. Related: [[qwik-proxy-idb-clone]] (saved tools JSON-snapshot before IDB put).

content.text:
The full loop is built. When a paragraph is giving the writer trouble, a tool now opens in the right margin beside that passage, Google Docs style. Tools can be kept and reused from the left margin, and the rubric panel is simplified. Type-check, lint and the client build are clean, and 33 new tests pass. **I haven't clicked through it in a real browser**, because the Chrome extension wasn't connected. The dev server compiles and serves the editor with the new code, but none of the interaction has been seen working.

**How it works**
- **Noticing trouble:** while the writer types, a local tracker counts how each paragraph is being edited. It watches for one sentence reworded over and over, sentences split and joined, qualifiers like "perhaps" added then removed, and stalling after cuts. It keeps no draft text beyond the paragraph's last few versions, in memory, and sends nothing while they type.
- **Confirming it:** on a pause, if a paragraph crosses the threshold, one Jev call checks that a tool would actually help. If Jev is unreachable, only a strong local signal can open a tool. Quick review and this now share one rate budget, so together they can't make more calls than before.
- **The four tools**, built on json-render's catalog with our own Qwik renderer:
  - **Sentence Lab:** your earlier wordings of the sentence plus variants from your own model. Pick or edit one in a working copy, click **Use this**, and undo restores yours.
  - **Rhythm Strip:** a bar per sentence showing its length against an adjustable range. Hover a bar to highlight its sentence; no model involved.
  - **Claim Check:** the paragraph's main claim with slots for a source, an example and a number. **Find** sends it to the Apparatus research.
  - **Reader Questions:** questions a reader would ask next, from a reader you can describe. Tick them off, or **Jot** one into your scraps.
- **Margins:** the right margin holds the live tool, level with its passage and joined by a hairline. The left margin shows **Your tools** plus a faint tick beside paragraphs you've worked hard on. On narrow windows the tool opens as a popover instead.
- **Keeping tools:** "Keep this tool" saves its settings (the length range, the support slots, the imagined reader), never the passage text.
- **Staying quiet:** one tool at a time. Dismissing a tool quiets that paragraph for 5 minutes. Tools are hidden in zen mode and for commenters, and a **Margin tools on/off** toggle sits next to "Pause review".

**Rubric and Writing tools**
- The rubric header now shows one score and one line: "Weakest: X — **Work on it in the draft**". That link closes the board and opens the matching tool on the passage live review flagged first.
- The second score and scoring method moved into a collapsed **How this was scored** section, which shows the real arithmetic.
- Section separators are heavier.
- In Writing tools, the "What would you like to explore?" dropdown is now a grid of 8 visible cards.

**Things worth knowing**
- **Bug fixed:** typing a paragraph forward was being read as splitting and joining sentences, which would have opened Rhythm Strip constantly. There's a regression test for it.
- **json-render gap:** its `validate()` doesn't check each component's props against its own schema. `validateToolSpec` now re-checks them.
- **Existing test crash:** the three `ai-client` test files crash on load (`__EXPERIMENTAL__ is not defined`). They crash the same way with my addition removed, so it comes from the existing uncommitted changes.
- **Not done:** the Storybook stories from the plan, and committing. The new files are untracked alongside your existing work.

The best next step is a browser pass: reword one sentence 3–4 times and pause, then check the card lands beside it and "Use this" followed by undo works. The detection thresholds are my first guesses and will need tuning once you've used it.

 * The other half of this module matters more than the grading. Every raw
 * answer — score, confidence and the **full probability distribution** — is
 * cached. Weights, thresholds and confidence floors are then applied over that
 * cache by pure functions. Moving a slider re-renders the report with no
 * inference, no network and no cost, which is what makes a threshold something
 * a writer can learn by dragging instead of guess at once in a settings page.
 */

import type { RubricCriterionSpec } from "../types";
import {
  isScore,
  isBimodal,
  modalLevel,
  scoreOutOf,
  score as scoreQuestion,
  estimateCost,
  type ScoreQuestion,
  type SystemOneAnswer,
  type SystemOneUsage,
} from "./system-one";
import { clampWeight } from "./rubric-criteria";

/** Twyne's criteria are scored out of 10, matching `RubricCriterion.maxScore`. */
export const CRITERION_MAX = 10;

/**
 * The ladder, worst-first. Five levels rather than eleven: Jev returns a
 * probability-weighted value *between* levels, so the resolution comes from
 * the distribution, not from the number of rungs. Asking for eleven would
 * spread mass thinly and depress confidence without adding signal.
 *
 * The wording is deliberately about the reader's experience rather than about
 * a grade, because the model is being asked to predict a reaction.
 */
export const SCORE_LEVELS = [
  "Poor — a serious weakness a reader would notice immediately",
  "Weak — noticeably below standard",
  "Adequate — acceptable but unremarkable",
  "Strong — clearly well executed",
  "Excellent — a distinct strength of the piece",
];

/* ── Building the request ──────────────────────────────────────── */

/**
 * One Score question per enabled criterion. `engagement` is excluded for the
 * same reason `weightedCriteriaScore` excludes it: it is derived from the
 * combined grade, so scoring it here would make the grade partly a function of
 * itself.
 */

content.text:
I've rewritten the rubric copy in plain language. Each piece of feedback now leads with the finding, uses one number only where it helps, and ends with something to try. Type-check, lint and the client build pass, and the rubric test suites pass (4 new copy tests, 2 new question-wording tests). I haven't viewed the panel in a browser.

**Before → after**

| Where | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Summary under the grade | "Harshest reader: devil scored 3/10. "The opening…" (cut off at 120 characters, showing a raw persona id) | "Getting there. Devil's Advocate is hardest to convince (3/10)." (always fits) |
| Rhythm | "Average sentence is 23.4 words, with a standard deviation of 3.1. A healthy mix lives in 12-22 word sentences with variance of 5-10." | "Your sentences average 23 words, and most are about the same length. Mixing in some shorter ones will give the reader a beat." |
| Word choice | "Type-token ratio: 31.2% (4.6 average word length). Healthy range: 35-60%." | "About 31% of your words are different words. That's a lot of repetition — look for the words you lean on." |
| Off-brief note | "Capped at 4.4/10: this measures shape, not substance, and target fit is only 2/10…" | "This score is held at 4.4/10 or below because the draft is off brief (2/10)…" |
| An editor fails to answer | "The draft is partial; the work to come is the interesting part." (shown as a real 5/10 verdict) | "This editor couldn't be reached, so this 5/10 is a placeholder, not a reading." |

**Criterion names:** Target Fit → **On brief**, Thesis & Argument → **Argument**, Bullshit Resistance → **Straight talk**, Pacing & Rhythm → **Rhythm**, Vocabulary & Diction → **Word choice**, Reader Engagement → **Reader pull**. The other names are simplified the same way, and each description is now a plain question, e.g. "Do sentence lengths vary enough to keep the reader moving?"

**Panel layout and labels**
- Each criterion row shows a word before its score: "Rhythm · uneven 4.2/10".
- Expanding a row shows what the criterion checks, what was found, and a "Try this" step. The "Try this" steps are rewritten and shared with the Full report page.
- Tabs are now **Criteria · Editors · Passages** (were Marks · Room · Review).
- Button and label text is plainer: "Grade this draft", "Grade again", "Ask the editors", "Needs most work: …", "Change what's graded", "How much each counts". "How this was scored" is also rewritten.
- The measured-style notes on the Full report page are in the same voice now ("Some padding: 2 sweeping claims with nothing behind them…").

**Things worth knowing**
- **Grades stay comparable:** criterion names and descriptions were also the wording of the question the scoring model is asked. I kept that question text as it was, so grades from before and after this change still compare. A test pins that wording.
- **Landing page:** it still says "A Target Fit judge…". I left the marketing copy alone; say if you want it matched.
- **Existing test crash:** the landing test crashes on load with `__EXPERIMENTAL__ is not defined`, the same error as the `ai-client` tests. It crashes without my changes too.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/diogenes/.claude/plugins/cache/typesafe-ai/typesafe/0.5.7/skills/typesafe-ai

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.

measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near

acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Models

Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first [System One model](/concepts/system-one). Every model on this page is served by the same endpoint, `POST /v1/systemone`. The request's `model` field selects which one handles the call; see the [API reference](/api) for the full request shape.

## Current models

| Jev 1.13                    | `jev-1.13.0`                                                                              |
| :-------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Price (per Btok / per Mtok) | \$42 / \$0.042                                                                            |
| Rate limits                 | 250,000 tokens per second / 1,200 requests per minute                                     |
| Context length              | 64k tokens per request; 32k tokens for `state` plus the longest question                  |
| Input                       | Text only. String, JSON object, or array of text values. No image, audio, or video input. |

* **Price:** Charged per input token. Output tokens are free. A Btok is a billion tokens and an Mtok is a million tokens.
* **Rate limits:** Measured in tokens per second and requests per minute. A request over either limit returns `429 Too Many Requests`. Our [client SDKs](/sdk) retry with backoff by default and honor the `retry-after` header when the response carries one. If you call the HTTP API directly, see [Handling rate limits](/api#handling-rate-limits).
* **Context length:** Jev ingests the `state` once and evaluates every question against it in parallel. The 64k budget covers the `state` plus all questions combined; the 32k budget applies to the `state` plus the single longest question. See [Speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out) for packing many questions into one request, and [Jev 1.13 jaggedness](/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13) for how accuracy shifts as the state grows.
* **Input:** Jev evaluates natural-language text. Pre-process non-text inputs (images, audio, video, binaries) into text or structured fields before sending them as `state`. See [State](/concepts/state) for supported shapes.

<Warning>
  **Rate limits are adjusting dynamically.** We are serving a very large volume of demand, and the limits above can change without notice while we do, as upcoming large GPU deals land and we let in more users. Once things settle down more, we'll be able to offer more stable limits. Higher limits are available on custom and enterprise plans. Contact [sales@typesafe.ai](mailto:sales@typesafe.ai).
</Warning>

## Aliases

An alias is a model name that resolves to a versioned model ID. Send it in the `model` field like any other name.

| Alias         | Points to    | Meaning                                                                                                                       |
| :------------ | :----------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `jev-latest`  | `jev-1.13.0` | The most recent stable, official release. The default in our client SDKs, and the name the examples in these docs use.        |
| `jev-preview` | `jev-1.13.0` | The most recent release, whether or not it is an official one. Moves ahead of `jev-latest` when a preview build is available. |

<Warning>
  `jev-preview` currently points to the same model as `jev-latest`. There is no preview build available right now.
</Warning>

An alias moves when a new release ships, so the answers behind it can change without a change on your side. The response's `model` field reports the versioned ID that answered, so you can log which model produced each result. If you have tuned confidence thresholds against a specific version, pin that version's ID instead of the alias and move to the new one on your own schedule.

## Customizing Jev

Jev is not fine-tuned or LoRA-adapted with customer data. It is trained with [RLCD](/introduction/machine-learning-primer) to return calibrated decisions, and the same weights serve every account. You shape its answers to your domain through the request rather than through per-account weights:

* Put your proprietary content, records, and reference material in the `state` field. See [State](/concepts/state).
* Encode your domain rules and boundary cases in the `instructions` and `criteria` of each question. See [How to build with TypeSafe](/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) and [Advanced: structure](/primitives/advanced).
* Decompose broad judgments into atomic questions and combine the outputs in code. See [Composite scoring](/patterns/composite-scoring) and the [AutoResearch cookbook](/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery) for training a downstream classical model on Jev's probabilities.

## Language support

Jev accepts natural-language text. English is the primary training language and where accuracy is currently best. Other languages, including CJK scripts, are handled but not equally well; test on your own content before relying on Jev for a non-English workload, and pay close attention to [Confidence](/confidence) when routing.

## Data handling

Jev is not trained on customer requests or responses. See [Legal](/legal) for the Data Processing Agreement, the Privacy Policy, and details on zero data retention (ZDR) for enterprise customers.

## Listing models

`GET /v1/models` returns the names your account can send in the `model` field, with a description and release date for each. It currently lists the aliases. Versioned IDs such as `jev-1.13.0` are accepted by the `model` field whether or not they appear in the list.

<CodeGroup>
  ```bash cURL theme={null}
  curl https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/models \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY"
  ```

  ```python Python theme={null}
  from typesafe_sdk import TypeSafeClient

  with TypeSafeClient() as client:
      for model in client.models.list().models:
          print(model.name, model.release_date, model.description)
  ```

  ```typescript JavaScript theme={null}
  import { TypeSafeClient } from "@typesafe-ai/sdk";

  const client = new TypeSafeClient();
  const models = await client.models.list();

Kev-4B is on Hugging Face. Its author calls it a **decision model**, not a "judgment model," but it's the model you're looking for.

## What it is
The main repo is **jaredpalmer/kev-4b**. You give it one document (the "state") and a set of typed questions. In a single forward pass it returns a probability distribution for each question, and it doesn't generate text. It's a LoRA adapter (r=16, 33.8M trainable parameters) plus a pointer head on Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B-Base (revision 1001bb4d), and it serves TypeSafe's public /v1/systemone contract.

## Latest version
The current version (2026-09-24, second update) is a "skills delta": the round-8 Kev-4B plus one more epoch (lr 2e-5) on 11,320 new training records, mixed with 4,000 replayed decision-v7 records. 6,000 of those come from hard-v1, a programmatically labelled set covering the skills Kev was worst at: long policy documents with exceptions and sublimits, trade-offs under stated priorities, probability and expected value, multi-hop reasoning over several facts, dates and arithmetic, judging a proposed answer, and abstaining when a fact is missing.

## Performance
- The author calls it "the recommended Kev," with the best accuracy per byte: 0.797 out of domain on the development partition, 0.837 on the locked test, a test Brier score of 0.255, and 0.77–0.78 on held-out rule pairs.
- An optional flag, KEV_DATE_FACTS=1, adds one sentence for each pair of absolute dates found in the state. With it, deadline accuracy goes from 0.60 to 0.85 and overall out-of-domain accuracy from 0.797 to 0.820.
- Trade-offs from the update: MMLU-Pro fell from 0.500 to 0.490. Coverage at ≤5% error stayed the same, and confident errors dropped from 8.2% to 6.9%.

## Model family and demo
The GitHub repo (jaredpalmer/kev) recommends starting with Kev-4B. Move up to Kev-9B if you have a bigger GPU, or to Kev-27B if you have an 80 GB GPU and want the most accurate version. Use Kev-0.8B when size matters more than accuracy. On new sources, Kev-27B comes within a point of Jev (0.848 vs 0.857), and Kev-4B and Kev-9B are within four points. There's a browser demo at huggingface.co/spaces/jaredpalmer/kev.

## Community GGUF ports
- **espetro/kev-4b-gguf**: the pointer head and calibration temperature are built into the file, which was made from the taigrr/kev-4b-gguf bundle (jaredpalmer/kev-4b checkpoint). For browser use, q8_0 is the only recommended quant, because q4 drifts enough to break the calibration. Its model card calls the model "Kev-0.8B" while also describing a 4B backbone, so check which one you're getting.
- **mys/kev-4b-GGUF**: these files are not standard llama.cpp GGUFs. They're built with ggmlc, and loading them in llama.cpp will fail. It's licensed Apache 2.0, the same as jaredpalmer/kev-4b.
- **DreamBlooms/kev-4b-GGUF** is another GGUF port.

content.content:
# Kev Small Jev-like decision models you can train and run yourself.

Kev is a family of small decision models built on Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 and based on the architecture described in [Jev's Architecture Unmasked](https://archerhume.com/posts/jevs-architecture-unmasked). You can use the pretrained weights or train your own. The API matches TypeSafe's [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api), so you can point their Python SDK at your local server. ## Highlights - Yes/no (`noul`), multiple-choice (`choice`) and rating (`score`) questions in one request. The questions share the text but can't read each other. - Calibrated probabilities by default: each checkpoint ships with a temperature fitted on held-out data. - Drop-in for Jev: the TypeSafe Python SDK works against a Kev server unchanged. - Four sizes, from a 0.8B that runs on a laptop to a 27B for a single data-centre GPU. - Fine-tune on your own labelled examples. A coding-agent skill runs the whole loop on Modal, from finding your questions to serving the result. - Deploy your own HTTPS endpoint with one command. It scales to zero when idle. - Try it in the browser first: [huggingface.co/spaces/jaredpalmer/kev](https://huggingface.co/spaces/jaredpalmer/kev). ## Models Start with Kev-4B. Move to Kev-9B if you have a bigger GPU, or to Kev-27B if you have an 80 GB GPU and want the most accurate Kev. Use Kev-0.8B when size matters more than accuracy. | Model | Base | Accuracy: New Sources | Accuracy: Trained Sources | Brier: New Sources | Runs on | Model Card | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | [Kev-0.8B](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-0.8b) | Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base | 0.648 / 0.697 | 0.827 / 0.838 | 0.481 / 0.416 | Any Apple Silicon Mac, L4 | [Details](docs/model-cards/kev-0.8b.md) | | [Kev-4B](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b) | Qwen3.5-4B-Base | 0.817 / 0.838 | 0.873 / 0.865 | 0.269 / 0.242 | 32 GB Mac, L40S, H100 | [Details](docs/model-cards/kev-4b.md) | | [Kev-9B](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-9b) | Qwen3.5-9B-Base | 0.822 / 0.852 | 0.872 / 0.874 | 0.286 / 0.237 | 32 GB Mac, L40S, H100 | [Details](docs/model-cards/kev-9b.md) | | [Kev-27B](https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-27b) | Qwen3.8-27B (post-trained) | **0.848 / 0.896** | 0.866 / 0.870 | **0.236 / 0.164** | B200, H200, H100 80 GB | [Details](docs/model-cards/kev-27b.md) | | Jev | Hosted | 0.857 / – | 0.845 / – | 0.211 / – | TypeSafe's API | – | Each cell is **development / test**. "New sources" means datasets and policy rules Kev never saw during training. It is the closest thing here to your own questions. "Trained sources" means held-out examples from the datasets Kev was trained on. We pick checkpoints using the development sets and read each test set only once per released model. Jev has only been run on the development sets. Brier scores the whole probability distribution, not just the top answer; lower is better. On new sources Kev-27B is within a point of Jev (0.848 vs 0.857), and Kev-4B and Kev-9B are within four points. We don't know what Jev was trained on, so this isn't a controlled comparison of the two architectures. [What to Expect](#what-to-expect) says where Kev is as good as Jev and where it isn't. Kev-0.8B, 4B and 9B start from Qwen base models and share one training recipe. Kev-27B starts from Qwen's post-trained release, and we don't know what that was trained on. Each model card has the full recipe, all results, and the earlier versions kept as Hub tags. The weights are also in the [GitHub release](https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/releases/tag/kev-family), with SHA-256 checksums. ## Quick Start ### Try It in the Browser The [Hugging Face Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/jaredpalmer/kev) runs Kev-4B and Kev-0.8B, with nothing to install. ### Run It Locally You'll need Python 3.12 or 3.13 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The repo's `.python-version` makes `uv sync` use 3.13; torch has no wheels for 3.14 yet. ```bash git clone https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev.git && cd kev uv sync --extra serve uv run --extra serve python -m kev.serve --run jaredpalmer/kev-4b --port 8009 ``` This starts Kev-4B on your machine: CUDA or ROCm if you have a GPU, MLX on Apple Silicon. /**
 * Tool-calling + analysis eval for a small local model (e.g. LFM2.5-2.6B),
 * the candidate engine for signed-out / free mode.
 *
 * Every other script in `evals/` talks to the hosted Portkey gateway with a
 * bare system+user body and never passes `tools`. None of them can answer the
 * only question that matters for a 2.6B on-device model: *can it drive the
 * `quote_passage` tool?* That tool is what pins an editor's note to a real
 * passage; a model that cannot call it produces unanchored notes, which is a
 * different (worse) product, not a slightly weaker one.
 *
 * So this script runs the REAL production path rather than an approximation:
 * the prompts from `convex/agentPrompts`, the tool from `convex/agentTools`,
 * `generateText` with `stopWhen: stepCountIs(3)` exactly as
 * `src/utils/ai-client.ts` does. What it changes is only the endpoint.
 *
 * Two runs per case, so tool competence and analysis competence are separable:
 *   - `tools`   — the real path, with `quote_passage` offered.
 *   - `notools` — same prompts, no tool. The control. If analysis is fine here
 *                 and collapses in `tools`, the tool is the problem, not the
 *                 model's reading of the draft.
 *
 * Output is written to two places:
 *   - `evals/local-model-scores.json` — per-case tool metrics + the aggregate.
 *   - `evals/local-model-runs.json`   — `{case_id, output}[]`, the exact shape
 *     `evals/judge.ts` reads. Copy it over `evals/runs.json` and run
 *     `bun run eval:judge` to score analysis quality against the same
 *     faithfulness/helpfulness rubrics used for the hosted models, so the
 *     small model is compared on the incumbent's terms.
 *
 * Serving the model — anything OpenAI-compatible works. llama.cpp needs
 * `--jinja` or it will not emit tool calls at all:
 *   llama-server -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF --jinja -c 8192
 *
 * Usage:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1 bun run eval:local
 *
 * Env:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL  default http://localhost:8080/v1
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_ID        default LFM2.5-2.6B
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_API_KEY   default "local" (llama.cpp ignores it)
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_TIMEOUT   ms, default 180000 — CPU decode is slow, be patient
 *
 * Read-only w.r.t. the repo otherwise: only writes the two files above.
 */

---
name: codex-image-generation
description: "How to generate Twyne's photographic assets with the codex CLI, plus the two flags that make it work non-interactively"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: a40cae62-e36f-4e91-ac80-373df93f64db
  modified: 2026-09-01T02:02:55.490Z
---

`codex exec` can generate images — the `image_generation` feature ships stable
and enabled (`codex features list | grep image_generation`), and auth is the
existing ChatGPT login (`codex login status`).

Two flags are required when driving it from a script, and neither is obvious:

```bash
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --skip-git-repo-check --cd "$OUT" \
  "Use your built-in image generation tool to create ONE <aspect> image and
   save it as ./<slug>.png in the current directory. Subject: … Style: …
   Do not write code, do not install packages." < /dev/null
```

- **`--skip-git-repo-check`** — without it: *"Not inside a trusted directory"* and it exits.
- **`< /dev/null`** — without it, it blocks on *"Reading additional input from stdin"* even though a prompt was passed as an argument.

Codex writes to `~/.codex/generated_images/<uuid>/exec-<id>.png`, then copies to
the path you named. Sizes top out at **1536 on the long edge** (1024×1536,
1536×1024, 1024×1024) — plan crops around that, never upscale on disk.

**Prompt discipline:** never ask for legible text. Body copy renders as
convincing gibberish, which is exactly what you want for paper texture; asking
for real words produces mangled letterforms instead.

The house style that produced a coherent six-plate set for the landing page:
*muted warm tungsten light, shallow depth of field, aged cream paper, vermilion
as the only saturated accent, film grain, no legible text, no faces, no modern
electronics, no logos.* Output was genuinely on-brand for Twyne's editorial
register — dark walnut desks, aged manuscript, red proof marks.

Optimise with the already-installed `sharp` (v0.34.5). ESM can't resolve
`sharp` from a script outside the project — import it by absolute path
(`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/node_modules/sharp/lib/index.js`) or run the
script from inside the repo. webp q78 suits these photographs; drop to q68 for
dense handwriting, which compresses badly (232KB → 184KB with no visible loss).

See [[landing-photo-essay]].
  -m, --model <MODEL>
  -s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>
      --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
      --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust
  -C, --cd <DIR>
      --json
